title: Promises and async/await
summary: Some jobs take time, such as loading a file. JavaScript can wait for a result without stopping every other job.
introduction: Some jobs take time, such as loading a file. JavaScript can wait for a result without stopping every other job. Think of ordering a snack and doing something else while it is made. Meet promises and use await to read the steps clearly.
learningObjectives: Explain why asynchronous code is needed and how the event loop orders it
Create promises and consume them with then, catch and finally
Write async functions and handle their errors with await and try/catch
Run independent tasks in parallel with Promise.all and Promise.allSettled

blocks.text: `setTimeout(fn, ms)` asks the browser to call `fn` after at least `ms` milliseconds. It does not wait; the script continues immediately, and the callback runs only when the current code has finished and the timer has expired. Even with a delay of `0` the callback comes after everything else in the script, because queued work can only start when the call stack is empty. That queueing mechanism is the **event loop**.

blocks.text: A **promise** is an object that represents a value that is not available yet. It starts *pending* and later becomes either *fulfilled* with a value or *rejected* with an error, exactly once. You attach what should happen next with `.then(onFulfilled)`, handle failures with `.catch(onRejected)` and run cleanup with `.finally()`. Each `then` returns a new promise, so they chain, and a value returned from one handler becomes the input of the next. The example wraps `setTimeout` in a promise; `fetch` and most modern browser APIs return promises directly.

blocks.text: The event loop has two queues. Promise reactions go into the **microtask** queue, which is drained completely as soon as the current script finishes. Timers, events and other callbacks wait in the **task** queue and run only after the microtasks. That is why a promise that is already resolved still logs *after* the synchronous code, but *before* a zero-delay timer.

Marking a function `async` makes it return a promise, and inside it `await` pauses the function until a promise settles, giving you the fulfilled value or throwing the rejection as an ordinary error. The surrounding page is not blocked: only this function waits. Errors are handled with the same `try`/`catch` as synchronous code, which is the main reason async/await replaced long `then` chains.

blocks.title: Forgetting await
blocks.text: Calling an async function without `await` gives you the promise, not the value: `const user = fetchUser(1); console.log(user.name)` prints `undefined`. The same mistake inside `try` means a rejection is not caught, because the function returned before the promise failed. If a value looks like `Promise {<pending>}` in the browser's developer tools (this site's console panel prints a promise as `{}`), an `await` is missing.

`await` one after another runs tasks sequentially, so three 100 ms requests take 300 ms. When the tasks are independent, start them all and wait once with `Promise.all`, which resolves to an array of results in the original order and takes as long as the slowest task. It rejects as soon as any task rejects; `Promise.allSettled` instead waits for all of them and reports each outcome, which suits dashboards where one failed widget should not hide the others.

blocks.title: Try it
blocks.text: Write `withTimeout(promise, ms)` that uses `Promise.race` to reject with `new Error("timeout")` if the promise takes longer than `ms`. Test it with the `wait` helper and both a short and a long delay.

questions.question: Where can the await keyword be used?
questions.explanation: await works inside functions marked async and at the top level of ES modules. In a regular function or a classic script it is a syntax error.
options: Only inside async functions and at the top level of modules

questions.question: `Promise.all` rejects as soon as one of the promises passed to it rejects.
questions.explanation: Yes: a single rejection makes Promise.all reject immediately with that reason. Use Promise.allSettled when you need every outcome regardless of failures.
